The Newfoundland fishing community
column2: Fisherfolk, mariners, and merchants from many nations crowded the Grand Banks off Newfoundland, swapping tales of Portuguese voyages, John Cabot's search, and Columbus's discovery.

column1: The characteristics of fifteenth-century European society
column2: Fifteenth-century Europe was isolated and backward, with about 90 percent of people living in scattered villages and working the land amid chronic food shortages and catastrophic disease.

column1: How Europe depended on Muslim middlemen
column2: Before the fifteenth century, western Europeans relied on Muslim merchants and mariners to bring the goods and learning of Asia and sub-Saharan Africa overland to Europe.

column1: The motives for European exploration
column2: Europeans explored to reach Asian riches directly without Muslim middlemen, gain gold and new markets and land, spread Christianity against Islam, and win glory for rival monarchs.

column1: The achievements that made the Age of Exploration possible
column2: Exploration rested on political nation-states, economic recovery after the Black Death, military armies and navies, and navigational technology such as caravels, lateen sails, and astrolabes.

column1: How the Black Death set the stage for expansion
column2: By killing so many Europeans, the Black Death eased population pressure and raised survivors' wealth, freeing capital for new technology, trade, and overseas ventures.

column1: How the Mediterranean Atlantic led to wider exploration
column2: Portuguese success on the Wine Islands with sugar and slave labor supplied profits, skills, and a plantation model that pushed exploration on to Africa, Asia, and the Americas.

column1: Why sugar plantations depended on slavery
column2: Because sugar required relentless planting, harvesting, and processing, planters turned to enslaved Africans as the cheapest and most controllable labor.

column1: How slavery developed along coastal West Africa
column2: Because strong West African states and deadly diseases blocked conquest, the Portuguese bargained with coastal rulers and bought enslaved Africans for Atlantic-island sugar plantations.

column1: The significance of Columbus's voyage
column2: Columbus's landfall linked two hemispheres that had developed separately for thousands of years, producing a world-changing encounter instead of the Asian trade route he expected.

column1: Why Spain conquered the Aztecs and Incas so quickly
column2: The Spanish won because of Indian allies who hated their unpopular rulers, divisions within the empires, smallpox epidemics, and Spanish firearms, steel weapons, and horses.

column1: The results of the conquest of Mexico
column2: The conquest destroyed the Aztec Empire, killed millions of Indians through war and disease, and made Mexico the wealthy center of Spain's American empire.

column1: Why disease was Spain's strongest weapon
column2: Because Native Americans had never encountered Eurasian diseases, virgin-soil epidemics of smallpox killed vast numbers and crippled resistance before and during conquest.

column1: How Spain governed its American empire
column2: Spanish monarchs soon replaced the independent conquistadors with an elaborate civil and church bureaucracy, so no colonial nobility could challenge royal authority.

column1: How American silver changed Spain and Europe
column2: American silver made Spain enormously rich and pushed Europe toward more capitalist economies and more centralized political authority, at the cost of many coerced Indian and African miners' lives.

column1: The elements of the Columbian Exchange
column2: The Americas gave the world maize, potatoes, squash, beans, tomatoes, and tobacco, while Europe and Africa brought horses, cattle, pigs, wheat, sugarcane, enslaved Africans, and smallpox and measles.

column1: What Protestant reformers criticized and taught
column2: Luther and Calvin attacked the Catholic Church's worldliness and corruption and taught that people were saved by divine grace alone and could read God's will in the Bible.

column1: How the Reformation shaped the colonization of America
column2: The Reformation turned European rivalry into religious war, so Catholic and Protestant powers treated colonies as outposts to defend their faith, and persecuted Protestants sought American refuges.

column1: Why Spain fortified Florida
column2: Spain founded St. Augustine to suppress French pirates, block French colonization, and keep Protestants away from the routes of its treasure fleets.

column1: Why England entered colonization late and then aggressively
column2: Barred from Spain's American preserve, English adventurers first fought religious wars and conquered Ireland, until fear of Spain and merchants' hunger for markets and land drove Elizabeth to colonize.

column1: Ireland as a model for English colonization
column2: England conquered Ireland before America, and veterans of the Irish campaigns brought its military, quasi-feudal methods and contempt for natives to Roanoke and the Chesapeake.

column1: Why Native leaders welcomed the first English colonists
column2: Native leaders such as Wingina tolerated the English because trade goods, weapons, and alliances with the newcomers might strengthen their own power.

column1: Why the Roanoke colony failed
column2: Historians blame Roanoke's failure on English leaders who demanded food while using violence against Wingina's people and on the Spanish Armada crisis that cut off the colony's supplies.

column1: How the European colonial empires differed
column2: The Spanish and French sent few settlers, ruled centrally, and worked to Christianize Indians, while England sent many settlers and made little missionary effort.

column1: England's position in the global race for empire by 1600
column2: By 1600 Portugal and Spain had built overseas empires, while England's failed experiments laid the groundwork for its renewed expansion in the seventeenth century.
